newsitem.title: USA: INSTANT VIEW - U.S. Nov retail sales down 0.4 pct.
newsitem.headline: INSTANT VIEW - U.S. Nov retail sales down 0.4 pct.

text.p: Following are comments from U.S. economists after the Commerce Department reported that November retail sales fell by 0.4 percent after a 0.2 percent rise in the prior month. Experts had expected retail sales to advance by 0.3 percent in November.
JAMES GLASSMAN, SENIOR ECONOMIST, CHASE SECURITIES INC: "It looks like consumer spending is not yet picking up as much as people had been hoping.
"The problem is that most people by the end of the day are going to say Christmas sales aren't over until Christmas is over. We have to wait and look at what the December figures look like."

MATTHEW ALEXY, CHIEF TREASURY MARKET STRATEGIST, CS FIRST BOSTON: "It means nothing for the Fed. For the economy the numbers mean modest growth and modest inflation. The numbers are pretty close to expectations. Total retail sales are less but the core number is pretty much on the screws. The numbers are slightly better than expected for the market."

KEVIN FLANAGAN, VICE PRESIDENT AND MARKET ECONOMIST, DEAN WITTER REYNOLDS: "Everyone was caught off guard by the weakness, so maybe you got more discounting than was initially thought. Some of the raw numbers from chain store sales and auto sales last week, I really didn't think pointed toward such weakness, especially in the overall figure.
"So maybe a little more discounting played a role here.
"No doubt a positive number for the (domestic money) market. It could cause some people to adjust their estimates of consumption for the fourth quarter, which could impact GDP statistics."
SAMUEL KAHAN, PRESIDENT, A.S.K. FINANCIAL RESEARCH: "The numbers are telling you that the economy has moderate forward momentum and that inflation remains under control.

"The weakness in automobile sales was a little bit of a surprise but given the volatility of that series, people will focus more on the total, excluding automobiles, which was up 0.3 percent. That tells you that consumer spending through November continues to be soft."
LARRY WIFP, ECONOMIST, NORWEST CORP: "I don't think it was totally unexpected.

"(It) may be ... the drop in the autos is probably more than expected. I still want to look ahead and think that we'll have a pretty good rebound in December with the Christmas season with some improvement in auto sales as well."
DAVID ORR, CHIEF CAPITAL MARKETS ECONOMIST, FIRST UNION CORP: "The retail sales figure might shift views that the Fed would be tightening to the view that the Fed eventually might have to ease.
"(But) the decline in November retail sales should be taken with a grain of salt due to the seasonal problem with late Thanksgiving.
"Excluding autos, October and November retail sales are up at a 5.5 percent annual rate compared to the third quarter. This is a decent rate, not overly troublesome."
